common_name: Étienne Soulange-Bodin Magnolia (Historic French Saucer Magnolia Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from hard late frosts that can blacken the earliest buds.

directions: Give this tree a permanent, open site, since it resents transplanting once established and takes several years to show its full flowering potential. The cultivar name honors French cavalry officer Etienne Soulange-Bodin, who first crossed Magnolia denudata with M. liliiflora at his estate at Fromont near Paris in the 1820s, producing the original soulangeana cross from which the entire group of saucer magnolias descends; this particular clone was formally named for him in 2000 from material believed to trace back to that original breeding work, though its exact identity to the historic tree is not fully settled. Its goblet-shaped flowers are white, stained rose-purple toward the base of each tepal, opening on bare branches ahead of the foliage. Mulch well and prune only to remove damaged wood.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Speciosa Saucer Magnolia (Late-Blooming Nearly-White Saucer Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Speciosa's later bloom window helps it avoid some of the frost damage that affects earlier-opening saucer magnolia cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil and allow room for an upright-growing small tree. Speciosa has been in the French and Belgian nursery trade since roughly 1830, making it one of the oldest surviving soulangeana selections, and it flowers late in the saucer magnolia season — around the same time as 'Brozzonii' — with nearly white tepals streaked purple on the outside. The late bloom timing is a practical advantage in regions with unpredictable spring frosts. Water deeply through the first two seasons and avoid heavy pruning.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Grace McDade Magnolia (Giant-Flowered Alabama Saucer Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; the unusually large flowers benefit from a site sheltered from strong spring wind.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun and give it room to spread into a broad small tree. Introduced in 1945 by Alabama nurseryman Clint McDade and probably a seedling of 'Lennei', Grace McDade produces some of the largest flowers of any saucer magnolia cultivar — ovate tepals to about 9 inches across, white flushed purple-pink at the base, opening on bare branches in early spring. The sheer flower size makes it a striking specimen tree once mature. Water deeply while young and prune only to remove crossing or damaged branches.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Chrysanthemumiflora Star Magnolia (Double-Flowered Japanese Star Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, in a site sheltered from the earliest hard frosts.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade and keep the root zone mulched. This Japanese cultivar was selected as a seedling of M. stellata 'Rubra' by nurseryman Koichiro Wada of Yokohama, and its many-tepaled, densely double flowers give the shrub a frilled, chrysanthemum-like bloom quite distinct from the simpler single-flowered star magnolia forms. It grows as a dense, rounded, multi-stemmed shrub that flowers at a young age. Water during establishment and avoid heavy pruning, which reduces next year's bud count.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Bred at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden and released in 1968, Evamaria was the breeding program's first successful cross between a North American magnolia species (M. acuminata) and an Asian one (M. liliiflora 'Nigra'), producing unusual purplish flowers tinged with orange, yellow, and green that set it apart from typical pink or white saucer-type blooms. It later became a parent of several further Brooklyn-bred yellow hybrids. Water regularly while establishing and prune only to remove damaged or crossing wood.

common_name: Hattie Carthan Magnolia (Yellow Magenta-Veined Brooklyn Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Released by the Brooklyn Botanic Garden in 1984 and named for Brooklyn tree-planting and community activist Hattie Carthan, this hybrid bears yellow flowers traced with magenta-rose veining, a distinctive departure from the plain yellow of many related Brooklyn hybrids. It forms an upright small tree that flowers reliably once established. Water deeply during the first few seasons, mulch to conserve moisture, and avoid hard pruning.

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the cold-hardy kobus parentage suits it to colder gardens than many hybrid magnolias.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade and give it room to grow into a multi-stemmed small tree. Marillyn is a cross of M. liliiflora 'Nigra' and the very cold-hardy M. kobus, bred at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden in 1954 but not formally introduced until 1989, named for benefactor Marillyn Wilson after the breeding program had already wound down. Its purple-magenta flowers open with contrasting white interiors in early to mid spring. Water during establishment and prune minimally beyond removing crossing or damaged branches.

common_name: Lois Magnolia (Late-Blooming Intense Yellow Brooklyn Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Lois blooms later than its sibling 'Elizabeth', which helps the flowers dodge late frost.

directions: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Lois is an unnamed sibling seedling of 'Elizabeth' crossed back to M. acuminata, bred at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden and only formally introduced in 1998, well after the original breeding program closed. Its flowers are a more intense, saturated yellow than 'Elizabeth' and open later in spring, giving it better late-frost avoidance. Water regularly while young and prune only to remove damaged or crossing wood.

common_name: Judy Zuk Magnolia (Columnar Dark Yellow Brooklyn Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; its narrow, columnar form suits tighter planting sites than most magnolias.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, allowing for a narrow but tall growth habit. Bred at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden from a complex cross involving M. acuminata, M. liliiflora, and M. stellata, this selection was introduced in 2007 and named for Judith D. Zuk, a former BBG president (1990-2005). Its dark yellow flowers are tinged with pink toward the base, and the tree's distinctly columnar form makes it useful where a narrow-footprint specimen is needed. Water deeply during establishment and prune only to remove damaged wood.
